performers: David Wise, violin; Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent
intro: A skylark on the solo violin: a cadenza played pianissimo, then folk-like tunes for flutes and oboe. David Wise and the Liverpool Philharmonic under Malcolm Sargent recorded Vaughan Williams’s Romance for violin and orchestra on 18 April 1947.

sections.label: Intro · Winds, muted strings, the cadenza
B · Second cadenza, then a tune for flutes
C · Trills, triangle and the oboe tune
B′ · The flute tune on the violin
sections.mNote: The flute melody, now played by the solo violin

cues.title: Winds, muted strings, then the soloist
cues.text: A short introduction for woodwind and muted strings leads to the soloist’s cadenza, marked pianissimo and sur la touche. The violin’s gently animated flurries evoke the song of a skylark.
cues.evidence: Philip Borg-Wheeler’s note for Hyperion (2014): a brief introduction for woodwind and muted strings, then a cadenza marked pianissimo and sur la touche, with gently animated flurries that evoke the skylark’s song. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Meredith’s lines in the score
cues.text: Vaughan Williams prefaced the score with three passages from the poem by his near-neighbour George Meredith, among them “He rises and begins to round, / He drops the silver chain of sound”.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note by Philip Borg-Wheeler, which quotes the lines the composer selected from Meredith’s poem. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604

cues.title: The 6/8 melody
cues.text: The orchestra comes in and the solo violin takes up the 6/8 melody that appeared near the end of the cadenza. Arabesques keep recalling the abandon of skylark song.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: “At the re-entry of the orchestra the solo violin takes up the 6/8 melody introduced towards the end of the cadenza”, with occasional arabesques. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Marie Hall’s Lark
cues.text: The Lark Ascending is dedicated to the violinist Marie Hall. She played the first performances: with the pianist Geoffrey Mendham at Shirehampton Public Hall, Bristol, on 15 December 1920, and with orchestra at Queen’s Hall the following June.
cues.evidence: Stephen Moss, The Guardian, 8 December 2020, on the Shirehampton première of 15 December 1920 and the Queen’s Hall performance of the following June; Hyperion note on the dedication. https://www.theguardian.com/music/2020/dec/08/the-lark-ascending-ralph-vaughan-williams-classical-chart-topper-jennifer-pike

cues.title: A second cadenza
cues.text: The orchestra drops out and the violin plays a second cadenza alone, shorter than the first.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia, “The Lark Ascending (Vaughan Williams)”: a second, unaccompanied cadenza, shorter than the first, leads to the flute episode, citing the Oxford University Press score of 1925, pp. 9–10; Hyperion note: another cadenza leads to a contrasting episode. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lark_Ascending_(Vaughan_Williams) https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune for flutes
cues.text: The cadenza leads to a contrasting episode, Allegretto tranquillo. The flutes sing a new melody while the violin plays around it.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: another cadenza leads to a contrasting episode (Allegretto tranquillo) with a new melody for flutes. Wikipedia, “The Lark Ascending (Vaughan Williams)”, gives the marking as Allegretto tranquillo quasi andante and cites the 1925 score, pp. 9–10. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lark_Ascending_(Vaughan_Williams)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Liverpool, 18 April 1947
cues.text: David Wise recorded this version with the Liverpool Philharmonic under Malcolm Sargent in the Philharmonic Hall, Liverpool, on 18 April 1947. Columbia issued it on two 78-rpm discs, DX 1386 and DX 1387.
cues.evidence: Columbia D.X. 1386 label (CAX 9863, “Conducted by Sir Malcolm Sargent”) in the Internet Archive item; Discogs release 27176142 (Columbia D.X. 1386 and D.X. 1387, recorded 18 April 1947 at Liverpool Philharmonic Hall) and the Internet Archive item’s description of the Columbia issue. https://archive.org/details/dx-1386-7-vw-lark-ascending https://www.discogs.com/release/27176142

cues.title: Trills and a triangle
cues.text: The Allegro tranquillo begins with solo violin trills and arabesques, punctuated by an off-beat triangle. The violin part takes firmer melodic shape in each new episode while keeping some of the skylark song.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: the Allegro tranquillo begins with solo violin trills and arabesques “now punctuated by off-beat triangle”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An oboe tune, scherzando
cues.text: The key moves to F major and the time to 6/8. Five bars in, the oboe plays a further new melody, marked scherzando.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: after the violin trills and triangle “the oboe plays a further new melody marked scherzando”. Wikipedia, “The Lark Ascending (Vaughan Williams)”: the key changes to F major, the time to 6/8, and the oboe enters after five bars. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lark_Ascending_(Vaughan_Williams)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The flute tune, now on violin
cues.text: The flutes’ melody returns, now played by the solo violin and marked Allegretto molto tranquillo, calmer than before.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: the flute melody “(now on solo violin and Allegretto molto tranquillo)” and the earlier 6/8 section return. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The 6/8 section returns
cues.text: After the flute melody on the violin, the earlier 6/8 section comes back.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: both the flute melody and “the earlier 6/8 section return”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violin alone
cues.text: The orchestra drops away and the violin plays on alone in skylark mode to the end of the piece.
cues.evidence: Hyperion note: the work “ends with the unaccompanied violin once more in skylark mode”. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W16127_GBLLH1748604
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: David Wise (violin), Liverpool Philharmonic Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: Both sources name the three. The Archive description adds a presumption that Wise was the orchestra’s leader; that is not independently established here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Romance for violin and orchestra; the orchestral version made in 1920, first played in June 1921.
fields.note: The Internet Archive description and the Discogs label credit call it a Romance for violin and orchestra. The performing edition is not identified, and nothing in the item points to cuts across its four sides.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Archive item gives September 1947 as the issue month. Discogs dates the UK set to 1947 and notes the “ST” tax code (April 1946 – November 1947).

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Matrices CAX 9863 to 9866, all first takes (four sides)
fields.note: Stated in the Archive item’s description. The labels and stampers were not examined for this dossier.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item is filed in that collection; no transfer engineer is named in the description.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive upload date (2 April 2022) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: FLAC original with a variable-bitrate MP3 derivative, joined from four 78-rpm sides into one file.
fields.note: Equalisation, speed correction and noise reduction are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Vaughan Williams’s copyright in the music runs to the end of 2028 in the UK and EU.
fields.note: The Vaughan Williams Foundation gives 2028 as the year copyright in his music expires. Composition rights are separate from the recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial issue in 1947, before 1963
fields.note: The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies to this 1947 Columbia set: its former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not United States or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

composer.died: 26 August 1958, Hanover Terrace, Regent’s Park, London
composer.epithet: He wrote down an Essex folk song in 1903, edited the English Hymnal and carried a Tudor psalm tune into the concert hall.
facts: Hubert Parry, Charles Wood and Charles Villiers Stanford in London and Cambridge; Max Bruch in Berlin, 1897; Maurice Ravel in Paris, 1907–08
Composer, folk-song collector, hymn-book editor, teacher and conductor; Leith Hill Musical Festival, 1905–53
Gustav Holst · Adeline and Ursula Vaughan Williams · Adrian Boult · Hubert Foss at Oxford University Press
Nine symphonies, operas, a masque for dancing, choral works, songs, hymn tunes, film scores and music for amateurs

quote.text: In the next world, I shan’t be doing music, with all the striving and disappointments. I shall be being it.
quote.source: Vaughan Williams to Sylvia Townsend Warner, about a fortnight before his death in August 1958, as she recorded it in a letter

composer.background:
On 9 February 1875 Arthur Vaughan Williams, vicar of All Saints, Down Ampney, died after a brief illness. His third child, Ralph, born in the vicarage on 12 October 1872, was two. His widow Margaret, a Wedgwood, took the children to her family’s house at Leith Hill Place in Surrey. Aunt Sophy gave the boy piano lessons, and at six he wrote a piece called The Robin’s Nest. He went to Charterhouse in 1887 and to the Royal College of Music in 1890, where Hubert Parry taught him composition; in 1892 he went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, to read history as well as music.

Adeline Fisher, a cellist and pianist whose first cousin was Virginia Woolf, became his wife on 9 October 1897 at All Saints, Hove, three days before his twenty-fifth birthday. After a brief spell of study with Max Bruch in Berlin he went back to his post as organist at St Barnabas, South Lambeth, which he had held since 1895, disliked, and gave up in 1899.
